evidence.label: A stable coordinate that is not a coordinate in four variables
An explicit noncoordinate polynomial with affine three-space zero fibre

headline: A polynomial that becomes a coordinate with one extra variable, but not without it, disproves two conjectures.
scope: The result is over the complex numbers, in four variables, with one added variable; three variables are not covered.
plain: A coordinate is a polynomial that some reversible change of variables turns into a single variable. This paper proves that one degree-five polynomial in four variables becomes a coordinate after adding one variable (Lean proof listed). It also proves that the same polynomial is not a coordinate in the original four variables. Every level set is a copy of three-dimensional space, yet none can be straightened into a flat slice. This disproves the stable coordinate conjecture in four variables and the Abhyankar–Sathaye conjecture in four-dimensional space.
doesNot: This does not settle the Abhyankar–Sathaye question in three variables, and it does not give a cancellation counterexample.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Shpilrain and Yu, stable coordinate conjecture
scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it disproves two named conjectures in the lowest dimension where the first could fail.

explanation:
Take the polynomial x + y² in two variables. Replace x by x − y², and it becomes plain x. That replacement is a polynomial automorphism [a change of variables made of polynomials that other polynomials can undo]. Here the undo step is x → x + y². Call a polynomial a coordinate if some such change turns it into one variable. A coordinate is one axis in disguise.

Now take four complex variables, x₁ to x₄. First set Q = x₂² − x₄² + x₁x₃. Then set f = x₁ − 2Q(Q(x₂ + x₄) + x₁x₄). Multiplied out, f has 16 terms and degree 5. At (0, 0, 0, 0) it equals 0. At (1, 0, 0, 0) it equals 1. At (1, 1, 1, 1), Q equals 1 and f equals −5.

Add a fifth variable, w, that f does not even use. The paper builds an explicit change of all five variables that turns f into x₁. It then proves that no change of the original four variables does this. So f is a stable coordinate [a polynomial that becomes a coordinate once spare variables are added]. Yet it is not a coordinate on its own. A Lean proof is listed for both halves.

The stable coordinate conjecture says this cannot happen. It predicts that a stable coordinate was a coordinate all along. Shpilrain and Yu stated the one-variable form as a conjecture in 2002. They also showed that it holds over the complex numbers in two and three variables. With one variable it is elementary. So four variables is the first place a counterexample could exist. One spare variable is already enough here.

The example also answers a second question. A fiber of f is the set of points where f takes one fixed value. For a coordinate, every fiber is a flat copy of affine three-space [ordinary three-dimensional complex space]. The paper shows every fiber of f is also a copy of three-space. Yet no change of variables of four-space carries any of them to a coordinate hyperplane. That is a flat slice such as x₁ = 0. Mathematicians call such a fiber nonrectifiable [impossible to straighten by any polynomial change of the whole space]. The Abhyankar–Sathaye conjecture predicts that this never happens. In two variables the Abhyankar–Moh–Suzuki theorem says the answer is yes. The example says no in four-dimensional space.

A companion paper from 24 September 2026 had already found a different counterexample to Abhyankar–Sathaye. Its polynomial F also has four variables, and the set where F = 0 is a copy of three-space. F fails to be a coordinate for a simple reason. At the point (2, 0, −1/2, 1/2), F equals −1 and all four of its slopes are zero. A coordinate can never have such a flat point, because the change of variables would then have no inverse there. That paper claims the three-space shape for the zero fiber only.

The October polynomial f cannot be caught by that test. It becomes a coordinate once w is added, and the same slope argument then rules out any flat point. That is the real obstacle. Earlier work found polynomials that become coordinates after adding variables. Lewis proved in 2013 that one well-known test polynomial, the second Vénéreau polynomial, is a coordinate. Blanc and Poloni later proved stability for a wider family. Showing that a polynomial is a stable coordinate is explicit work. Showing that it is not a coordinate needs a different kind of argument.

Here is the idea in plain terms. If f were a coordinate, a certain sliding symmetry would have to survive on a simpler ring built from f. The paper then shows that no such symmetry exists. One quantity in it would have to be a polynomial and also carry a negative weight. Both cannot be true. The strategy adapts an earlier OpenAI preprint on a related question, called cancellation. This example, however, does not itself give a cancellation counterexample. Its surrounding space is ordinary four-space, and the problem sits in the polynomial f.

Adding more unused variables keeps the Abhyankar–Sathaye failure in every dimension of four or more. The three-variable case is not covered. How sure is this? The Lean scope note lists a formal version of the main claims. It covers the degree-five polynomial and its coordinate status with and without w. It also covers the claim that every fiber is three-space and cannot be straightened. It also covers the Abhyankar–Sathaye failure in every dimension of at least four. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold. The Lean scope note lists formal versions of the main statements. No specialist has published a review, and the three-variable case is not addressed.
